The doctrinal evolution of civil rights and equal protection from Buchanan v. Warley (1917) through Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education (1971) is marked by significant legal standard transitions through intermediate precedent. 

Buchanan v. Warley (1917) (ID: 245_0060-01) established that a city ordinance forbidding colored persons from occupying houses in blocks where the majority of houses were occupied by white persons was unconstitutional, as it deprived property owners of the right to dispose of their property to constitutionally qualified purchasers. This case laid the groundwork for future civil rights and equal protection litigation.

In the years following Buchanan v. Warley, the Supreme Court continued to refine the legal standards for civil rights and equal protection. For example, in Daniels v. Tearney (1880) (ID: 102_0415-01) and Landsdale v. Smith (1882) (ID: 106_0391-01), the Court addressed issues related to property rights and equal protection, but these cases did not directly impact the evolution of civil rights doctrine.

The landmark case of Brown v. Board of Education (1954) (cited in Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education, ID: 402_0001-01) marked a significant turning point in the doctrinal evolution of civil rights and equal protection. Brown v. Board of Education held that segregation in public schools was unconstitutional, establishing the legal standard that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.

The Court continued to build upon this foundation in cases such as Raney v. Board of Education of Gould School District (1968) (ID: 391_0443-01), which held that the District Court's dismissal of the complaint was an improper exercise of discretion and that the district courts should retain jurisdiction in school segregation cases to ensure that a constitutionally acceptable plan is adopted and implemented.

In Green v. County School Board of New Kent County (cited in Raney v. Board of Education of Gould School District, ID: 391_0443-01), the Court further refined the legal standard, holding that a "freedom-of-choice" plan was not an adequate remedy to eliminate segregation in public schools.

Finally, in Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education (1971) (ID: 402_0001-01), the Court held that the pairing and grouping of noncontiguous school zones was a permissible tool to achieve desegregation and that transportation of students was a permissible means of implementing a remedial decree. This case marked a significant transition in the legal standard, as the Court recognized the need for proactive measures to achieve desegregation and equal protection in public education.

In conclusion, the doctrinal evolution of civil rights and equal protection from Buchanan v. Warley (1917) through Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education (1971) is characterized by a series of intermediate precedents that refined the legal standards for civil rights and equal protection. These cases, including Brown v. Board of Education, Raney v. Board of Education of Gould School District, and Green v. County School Board of New Kent County, collectively contributed to the development of the legal standards that ultimately led to the holding in Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education.
